title: Accumulator Safeguards & KV-cache Scaling — Proposal
content:
Purpose:

This doc collects observations from recent mixed-precision regressions, proposes a compact set of runtime/kernel changes and a KV-cache scaling policy aimed at reducing NaN/inf events and long-tail numeric drift in production streaming workloads. The goal is practical: minimize regressions during FP8/FP16 deployments with low perf overhead and clear rollout steps.

Background / problem statement:

- We've seen intermittent NaN/Inf events during long-running generation with FP8-backed models (mostly autoregressive large models, sequence lengths > 2k). Events cluster during bursty traffic where batching and KV-cache reuse interact.
- Root causes are multi-factor: limited accumulator precision (FP16/FP8), denorm flushing and underflow, accumulation overflow in contiguous kernel loops, and scale metadata mismatch when KV entries are re-quantized or reused across different scale regimes.
- Existing mitigations (global rescale at layer boundaries, stochastic rounding on some kernels) reduce but do not eliminate tail events; some fixes cause nontrivial perf regressions on A100/RTX-class instances.

Observations from recent experiments (summary):

- Small-scale stress harness (synthetic streaming tokens) reproduced NaNs by alternating high-attention-sparsity tokens with long-context repeated prefixes.
- Switching GEMM accumulation to FP32 for the first 256 reduction elements prevented NaNs in ~85% of runs but added ~9% latency on 80-token generation on A100.
- Recording per-kv entry scale metadata and refusing to reuse incompatible entries removed a subset of errors (KV-scale mismatch), but increased memory pressure and cache miss rate.
- Applying a conservative per-layer clamp to logits reduced NaN frequency but changed output distributions in subtle ways (affects logits-sensitive decoding like top-k sampling).

Key failure modes (concrete):

1) Accumulator saturation: repeated large-magnitude partial sums plus small float range (FP16 accumulator) cause rounding to Inf/NaN in FMA kernels when intermediate exponent overflows.
2) Denorm accumulation: very small values accumulated into large sums lose representation and create tiny denorms that later underflow unpredictably during requantization.
3) KV-scale drift: KV-cache entries captured under one quantization scale are later applied to inputs requiring a different scale; in-place requantization without proper metadata causes mis-scaling and eventual downstream instability.
4) Scheduling-induced batching: large dynamic batching increases reduction lengths and changes the reduction order, exposing accumulation pathologies not seen in small-batch microbenchmarks.

Proposed mitigations (ranked by expected impact / cost):

A. Adaptive accumulator precision window (kernel change)
- Idea: perform GEMM accumulation in FP32 for the first N reduction elements (N tunable, default 256), then continue accumulation in the configured accumulator type. This reduces overflow/denorm triggers for common head sizes while keeping most of the work in lower precision to preserve throughput.
- Implementation notes: add a switchable path in our matmul kernels with minimal branch overhead; microbench for N in {128,256,512} across hardware targets.
- Expected perf: ~5–12% latency hit depending on geometry; large win on numeric stability.

B. Per-layer dynamic rescale metadata and KV-cache-safe reuse policy
- Store a compact scale tag with every KV entry (16-bit or 8-bit encoded scale). When reusing a KV entry, check compatibility with current layer/request scale; if mismatch exceeds threshold T (e.g., factor > 2 or < 0.5), either:
  1) trigger a lazy re-quantization into the current scale with a fast path, or
  2) mark entry as stale and fall back to recomputation for that key (incremental penalty).
- For memory/perf tradeoffs, favor (1) for dedicated capacity and (2) for constrained environments.
- Small API change: add KV metadata header versioning so future scale policy changes are forward-compatible.

C. Scheduler-aware batching heuristics
- Scheduler should prefer small batch size for requests touching layers with recent numeric incidents. Add a lightweight per-model per-layer health score; if score > threshold, prioritize low-latency routing for that model until health recovers.
- Also add a burst dampener: when a request stream presents rapid sequence-length growth, temporarily cap batch assembly for that stream for M tokens.

D. Kernel numerical guards and safe-requant paths
- Add saturating FMA (clip to max finite before storing into accumulator) for pathological cases; prefer guard-on-exception rather than always-on clips to keep fast-path perf.
- Provide an opt-in "safe-requant" kernel used only during KV re-quantization or known risky transitions. It uses a two-pass approach: compute max absolute in block -> compute rescale -> requantize with rounding to nearest even or stochastic rounding.

E. Metrics, probes and automatic rollback triggers
- New telemetry: per-request numeric-health tags, per-layer NaN/inf counters, KV-scale-mismatch rate, accumulator-exponent-distribution histograms.
- Add automatic canary rule: if NaN rate > X per 10k tokens or per-layer drift > Y over 30 minutes, automatically divert a fraction of traffic to a higher-precision variant (fp16 accumulators -> fp32 accumulators) and raise alert.

Experiment plan / microbench harness:

- Harness enhancements: extend synthetic streaming harness to generate: (a) alternating repeated prefixes + random noise, (b) long-tail sequence elongation, (c) mixed scale inputs (simulate embeddings drawn from different quantization runs).
- Matrix of runs: models = {7B, 13B, 65B}, hardware = {A100-40G, A100-80G, H100 (early)}, precision = {fp8, fp16}, kernel variant = {baseline, adaptive-accum(N=128,256), safe-requant}. Capture: nan_count, tail_latency, memory, KV-hit-rate.
- Success criteria: NaN reduction >= 95% vs baseline with <=10% median latency regression.

Implementation plan and rollout:

1) Phase 1 (research): implement microkernel switch to support adaptive first-N FP32 accumulation and safe-requant prototype. Bench locally and push PR to runtime repo. (Owner: Evan; ETA: 3 weeks)
2) Phase 2 (canary): enable per-layer scale metadata +KV-scale-check in a canary dedicated cluster, route 1% traffic; track metrics for 2 weeks. (Owner: Li; ETA: 4 weeks)
3) Phase 3 (staged rollout): expose scheduler health-score and batch-dampener flags; gradual enable for models that saw incidents; compare customer-facing metrics pre/post. (Owner: Aisha; ETA: 6 weeks)
4) Phase 4 (opt-in release): expose safe-requant and adaptive accumulator to private deploy customers as opt-in flags; iterate on perf. (Owner: Platform Eng; ETA: Q2 next quarter)

Testing and QA:

- Unit tests: deterministic small-matrix tests that assert no NaNs for seeded ranges, exponent-limits checks and exactness tests for small N.
- Fuzz tests: random weight/activation generation including extreme exponents, run for 72 hours on CI GPU runners.
- Perf gates: tight microbenching with flame graphs to ensure hot-paths see <12% regression for default N.
- Regression suite: run on every PR against representative customer traces (anonymized), flag any increase in NaN/key-metric.

Operational considerations:

- Memory overhead: per-KV entry metadata increases memory by ~1–2%. We'll provide config knobs to compact encode scale metadata.
- Backwards compatibility: provide KV metadata versioning and a slow-path to handle older entries.
- Customer communication: prepare a short KB article describing opt-in flags and behavior changes for Private and Dedicated customers; include rollback instructions.

Open questions / tradeoffs:

- What is the acceptable default N for adaptive accumulation on diverse hardware? (need perf matrix)
- Stochastic rounding vs round-to-nearest: which is better for reproducibility across runs? Stochastic helps bias but harms determinism and complicates debugging.
- How aggressive should KV rejection be? Conservative rejection reduces risk but hurts cache efficiency and increases compute.
- Is safer always-on saturating math preferable to selective guard-on-exception path? Hardware specifics matter.

Appendix: small pseudocode for adaptive first-N accumulation (conceptual)

// conceptual pseudocode
function adaptive_matmul(A, B, N):
  acc = 0 (FP32)
  for i in 0..N-1:
    acc = acc + to_fp32(A[i]) * to_fp32(B[i])  // first window in FP32
  acc_low = to_accumulator_type(acc)
  for i in N..K-1:
    acc_low = acc_low + A[i] * B[i]  // continue in configured accumulator type
  return acc_low

(Exact implementation will inline and vectorize to avoid branching and reduce register pressure.)
